The hostel had to be empty by six, the rain was coming sideways, and Karthik's books were still in cardboard boxes going soft at the corners. Yogesh had come to help him move to his uncle's flat after he'd dropped out of the semester.

When Yogesh taped a box wrong, Karthik exploded. "You always do this! You think you're so helpful. You just like feeling better than me."

The words hit like a slap. Yogesh wanted to throw the tape down and leave him to it. Instead he took a breath, said, "Okay," and carried the box to the autorickshaw.

They finished at 5:50. In the auto Karthik stared out at the rain.

Two weeks later, over tea, Yogesh said quietly, "That day really hurt." Karthik looked down. "I know. I was angry at everything. Not you. Sorry."

qa.a: The hostel had to be empty by six.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when Karthik exploded, and what did he want to do?
qa.a: Yogesh felt hurt, as if slapped, and wanted to throw the tape down and leave.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Staying steady that day and raising the hurt two weeks later when calm worked, because Karthik could hear it and apologise.

qa.q: How might Karthik have seen that moving day?
qa.a: Karthik was likely overwhelmed and ashamed about dropping out, so his anger at everything spilled onto the friend helping him.

grounding: The story shows a young man whose friend lashes out during his lowest week, staying steady and raising the hurt later when both are calm.

Chinmay hadn't left his Andheri flat much since the startup he'd joined shut down. When Dhruv brought biryani on Thursday, Chinmay didn't say thanks. He said, "Did Pallavi send you? I don't need charity from people with real jobs."

Dhruv felt his face go hot. He had come after a twelve-hour shift. A sharp answer rose in his throat.

He put the parcel on the table instead. "Nobody sent me. I'll sit for a bit."

Chinmay turned back to his laptop. Dhruv scrolled his phone on the sofa for half an hour, then left.

On the train, Pallavi called. "How was he?" "Horrible," Dhruv said, and then, "But I think he's angry at the world, and I was the only one there." The next Sunday they both went back. Chinmay opened the door and said, "About Thursday. I was a jerk."

Irawati, come here, you're thinking about that boy who stopped replying to your messages, no? Let your old Pradeep uncle tell you something. When I was twenty, in engineering college, my friend Bhola wrote me three letters from his village. I was busy with exams and a new girl I liked. I didn't answer even one.

In March a classmate told me Bhola's father had died and Bhola had stopped eating properly. I felt sick with guilt. For a week I didn't write because I was embarrassed. What could I say after three unanswered letters?

Then I took the overnight bus. I stood at his door and said, "I'm sorry I didn't write. I'm here now." That's all. He made me tea. I stayed four days and helped in the fields. Guilt only helped when it made me get on that bus.

qa.a: Bhola may have felt surprised and comforted, and making tea suggests he welcomed his friend back despite the silence.

At the canteen Payal said, "You know Suraj's father lost his job? He's barely leaving his room."

Tejas's stomach dropped. He wanted to hide, to pretend he hadn't seen them. How do you reply a week late?

He borrowed Payal's phone. "Suraj, I only just saw your messages. I'm sorry I wasn't there. Can I come over now?" A long minute. Then: "ok."

He walked the two kilometres in the heat, with two cold drinks from the stall. They sat on Suraj's steps. Mostly Suraj talked. Tejas listened, and came back the next day too.

In the Bengaluru PG, Anand smiled at breakfast and then lay on his bed all afternoon with the curtains shut. For weeks the thoughts had got heavier: everyone else manages, I'm just weak, they'd be better off without me dragging them down. When his mother called he said, "All fine, Amma, busy with project."

On Tuesday Jomon, his roommate, found him still in bed at four. "Anand. You've not eaten. Talk to me."

Anand almost said he was just tired. Then something cracked. "I'm just a weight on everyone. It's too much. I can't hold it by myself anymore."

Jomon sat on the bed. He didn't argue. He said, "Then let's not hold it alone. Now, together." He looked up the helpline, and Anand spoke to a counsellor for half an hour with Jomon beside him. That evening Anand called his mother and told her the truth.

"Because I am fine."

"You haven't come to class in a week."

Pallavi looked at the tea. "Everyone else is managing, didi. You're managing. I'm just... I'm the weak one. I don't want to bother anyone."

"It's all in your mind," his father said. "Be strong. In my time nobody had these problems." He went back downstairs.

On Sunday Jeevan's uncle Hemant, a teacher whom his father respected, sat with them both. Hemant read the note aloud. His father listened, frowning. Then he said, "What do you need from us?"

"Arre, Ganga, it's all in your head. Just be strong, eat properly," her mother said, stirring the dal in their Kolkata flat. "Your cousin cleared her exams without all this drama."

Ganga went to her room and sat on the bed, shaking. She had spent a week working up the courage to say she was crying every day and couldn't get out of bed some mornings.

She messaged Keerthana: "Told Ma. She said it's in my head." Keerthana replied, "It's real whether she gets it or not. Want me to come with you to Dr Bose?"

On Saturday they went to the family doctor. Ganga described exactly what was happening: the crying, the mornings, the not eating. Dr Bose listened, then said, "Bring your mother next time. I'll explain it to her."

The following week her mother came, and asked quietly, "How long has it been like this?"

Counsellor's note, sessions 1-4, Rashmi.

Session 1: Rashmi sat on the edge of the chair with her bag on her lap and answered in single words. She said her parents didn't know she had come. She laughed whenever she mentioned anything painful.

Session 2: She arrived late and said she nearly didn't come because "this feels weird, talking to a stranger". I told her awkward is normal at this stage and that it is also fine to try another counsellor if we don't fit.

Session 3: She put the bag on the floor.

Session 4: She talked for twenty minutes about her grandmother's death last year, something she said she had never told anyone. She cried and did not apologise for it. At the end she said, "This is strange but it helps." We booked the next session.

- Damini

I'm Pooja and I almost didn't go back after the first session. It was so awkward. Pradeep, the counsellor, asked, "What brings you here?" and I talked about the weather in the waiting room for five minutes. I walked out thinking, this is a waste, I'm not a talking person.

Today he didn't push. He asked what my week was like and I ended up telling him about the panic on the metro. He didn't look shocked. He just said, "That sounds exhausting." And it was. It is. I cried a little, which was embarrassing, and also a relief.

I still don't know if he's the right fit forever. He said if not, he'd help me find someone else. For now I've booked session four.

I'm Tenzin, and last winter I disappeared into my room for most of a month. Nobody at college noticed except Arnab.

He knocked one Sunday with two plates of momos from the stall near the gate. I said I was busy. He said, "Okay, I'll eat mine here," and sat on the floor of my room. He didn't ask what was wrong. He talked a bit about his cricket team, then went quiet.

After a while I said, "I'm not doing well. I don't want to talk about it much." He nodded. "Tell me what you can. Anything I can do that's boring and practical?"

I almost laughed. My library books were overdue, the fine piling up. He took them back the next morning.

That Sunday was the first time in a long while that I felt seen. I let him keep coming on Sundays. It was easier than pretending.

Thank you for coming to the thirteenth-day ceremony. I didn't get to talk to you properly, so I'm writing.

Chaitanya

"Because I should have," Uday said. "Imran told me he was tired all the time. I said, 'Everyone's tired, yaar.' Two weeks later his heart just stopped. On the football field."

"Did anyone know he had a heart problem?"

"No. Not even his parents."

"So how could you?"

Uday was quiet. "I just wish I'd said something better."

"I think that wish is love, Uday. It just doesn't have anywhere to go now."

He pressed his palms against his eyes.

"What would you want to say to him?"

"That he was the funniest person I knew. That I'm sorry."

"Write it down. And come to the memorial circle on Friday. His other friends will be there."

qa.q: Where did Imran's heart stop?
qa.a: It stopped on the football field.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he kept saying "I should have"?
qa.a: Uday felt guilty and full of regret, blaming himself for missing something nobody knew.

qa.q: What did Salma suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Salma suggested writing to Imran and going to the memorial circle, which gives Uday's love and sorrow a place to go instead of self-punishment.

qa.q: How might Salma see Uday's guilt?
qa.a: Salma sees it as love with no outlet, not as proof Uday did something wrong, since nobody knew about Imran's heart problem.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young man replaying what he should have said before his friend died, and being helped to see guilt as love and share memories.
